title: Guru Ram Das's gurpurab
hookLine: his birth is marked in autumn with kirtan at Amritsar, the city he began

lines: AMRITSAR AT TWO IN THE MORNING.
ONE MAN, A POOL, A LOT OF DIGGING.
cards: Some people are remembered for what they said, some for what they built. A few are remembered for a place so alive it's hard to imagine the world without it.
Stand at the edge of the pool in Amritsar at two in the morning: the Harmandir Sahib glowing gold on the water, kirtan floating across, people walking the marble barefoot in the cool air.
It all began with one man, a pool, and a lot of digging. Today: sarovar.

teach.b: Guru Ram Das was born in Lahore and named Jetha. Tradition remembers him as an orphan who sold boiled grain on the street to get by.

He came to Goindval, served in the langar of the third Guru, Guru Amar Das, married his daughter, Bibi Bhani, and became the fourth Guru. You've met him already on this path: he wrote the four laavan.
His great work of building began with a pool.

teach.h: A POOL DUG, A TOWN GROWN.
teach.b: He had a sarovar, a sacred pool, dug out, and a town grew around it.
It was called Ramdaspur, Guru Ram Das's town, and later Amritsar, the pool of nectar. Tradition says he invited traders and craftspeople to settle there, and the town became a center of Sikh life.
His son Guru Arjan completed the pool and built the Harmandir Sahib in the middle of it.

Guru Arjan wrote, on Ang six twenty-five, in paraphrase: bathing in the pool of Ram Das, all the sins one has committed are washed away. Sikhs read that bathing as both outward and inward: the water, and the Name.
His gurpurab falls in the autumn, and on that day Amritsar is full. The Harmandir Sahib is lit, kirtan goes on through the day, and many come to bathe in the pool he began.
Sikhs often speak of him with a particular tenderness: the humble one, whose door is open to all.
A city, a pool and a wedding song: quite a legacy for a boy who once sold grain.

how: On Guru Ram Das's gurpurab in autumn, the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar is illuminated, kirtan continues through the day, and many pilgrims bathe in the sarovar he began.

a sacred pool beside a gurdwara

games.q: you're Guru Ram Das and want a center for the Sikhs. where does the story say you begin?
o: with a pool, dug out, and a town around it.
games.why: he had a sarovar dug; Ramdaspur grew around it, and the town became Amritsar.

practice: Close your eyes and see the dark, still water, a golden building at its center and its reflection beneath, kirtan carried across, people walking slowly around the edge, barefoot on cool marble.
Let your breath slow to their pace; if you've been there, remember it, and if not, let it be new. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you walk the edge in your mind.

wordCard.voice: Sarovar, the sacred pool Guru Ram Das had dug, around which Amritsar grew, marked each autumn with kirtan and light at the Harmandir Sahib.
